newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine Dirty War vets may give evidence.
newsitem.headline: Argentine Dirty War vets may give evidence.

text.p: Some Argentine military men who took part in human rights abuses in the Dirty War of the late 1970s may be ready to give evidence in Spain about the disappearance of 300 Spaniards, lawyers said on Tuesday.

Spanish Judge Baltazar Garzon has summoned more than 100 officers of the 1976-83 military regime, among them de facto President Jorge Videla and ex-navy officer Adolfo Scilingo, whose confession early last year to "death flights" over the River Plate triggered a spate of Dirty War mea culpas.

Spanish lawyer Angel Garcia Castillejo and Isabelo Barros, human rights secretary of Spanish opposition party Izquierda Unida, have been in Argentina collecting evidence and said the list of Spanish "disappeared" had grown to 300 from 266.
The newspaper Clarin on Tuesday quoted Barros as saying they had interviewed six Dirty War veterans, some of whom would give evidence in Madrid if their safety was guaranteed.

Scilingo, who told last year of flights in which thousands of suspected leftists detained and tortured at the Navy School of Mechanics were thrown to their deaths in the river, said on Tuesday he was prepared to give evidence in Spain.
"With all the caution you need in these cases, we believe these people who came forward as eyewitnesses or participants in acts of repression are credible," Barros told Clarin.
Garcia Castillejo told reporters on Monday he had "my hands and cases full of testimonies and documents and decisive proof to put the people responsible for the repression on trial."

Officially, 14,000 people died or "disappeared" in the Dirty War, but human rights groups say the number was 30,000. Culprits were tried after democracy returned but Radical Party President Raul Alfonsin let off all but senior officers and Peronist President Carlos Menem pardoned them all after he came to power in 1989.

Rights groups like the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo hope a Spanish trial will end in international arrest warrants to keep Dirty War criminals from travelling abroad, as is true of ex-navy Capt. Alfredo Astiz, the "Blond Angel," who was given a life sentence in absentia by France for killing two French nuns and is wanted by Sweden for killing a Swedish student.
"Argentina will be the jail of these torturers," said Nora de Cortinas, a leader of the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo.
